The Puaiohi (Myadestes palmeri) exhibits life-history traits shaped by the cool, wet microclimate of its montane forest habitat on the island of Kauai. Newly hatched chicks, altricial and brooded continuously by the female, have a wet weight at birth of 3.6 grams [Wwb = 3.6 grams], a remarkably modest mass that underscores the substantial energetic investment required to fledge a single offspring. Eggs are incubated for an average of 14.5 days [ab = 14.5 days] at a controlled nest temperature of 36 °C [T = 36 °C], a developmental period typical of small-bodied island thrushes. The incubation period is prolonged relative to some continental turdids, likely reflecting the cooler ambient conditions found in its high-elevation cloud forest range. This slow pace of embryonic development is consistent with a broader pattern of reduced reproductive rates observed in many endemic Hawaiian passerines, which often prioritize offspring quality over numerical output.

Field studies have documented that females typically lay 2 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = 2 eggs per clutch], a modest clutch size that may represent an adaptation to reliable but limited food resources in the understory. Breeding pairs produce on average 2.8 clutches per year [F_R_i = 2.8 clutches per year], which, when combined with the two-egg limit, results in a relatively low annual reproductive output compared to many mainland thrushes of similar body size. Under the thermal conditions typical of an adult's active metabolism, estimated at 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C], the nestling period culminates in fledging at 19.5 days after hatching [tx = 19.5 days after hatching]. This comparatively brief nestling phase is notable given the species' limited altricial development at hatching, but it may function to reduce predation risk in the vulnerable nest environment. The timing of this transition is critical for post-fledging survival.

Following fledging, the developmental trajectory of juvenile Puaiohi proceeds toward gonadal maturation. Puberty, defined by the onset of gametogenesis, is attained at 58.5 days after hatching [tp = 58.5 days after hatching] under the same thermal regime of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]. This represents a relatively rapid sexual maturation for a bird of its size, a characteristic that may be linked to the high adult mortality rates typical of isolated island populations. However, despite this early physiological readiness, behavioral observations indicate that most individuals defer actual reproduction. While birds can breed at one year of age, they normally do so at three years, a social constraint likely imposed by intense competition for limited high-quality nesting territories in the Alakai Swamp. The protracted delay between physiological puberty and effective first breeding reflects the species' reliance on stable, long-term pair bonds and the challenge of acquiring a suitable territory.

The selective pressures acting on juvenile dispersal and territory acquisition are reflected in the species' overall life-history pace. The maximum recorded lifespan for the Puaiohi, observed under the species' typical active metabolic temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C], is 7957 days [am = 7957 days], which equates to nearly 22 years. This impressive longevity is exceptional among small passerines and underscores a slow life-history strategy where high annual adult survival offsets a low annual fecundity. The ultimate wet weight attained by adults is 43 grams [Wwi = 43 grams], a body mass that places the Puaiohi among the larger members of the Hawaiian thrush radiation. This relatively robust size, combined with extended lifespan, enables individuals to allocate considerable energy to repeated reproductive attempts over many seasons.

The age at which a young bird first successfully produces its own brood is a pivotal demographic parameter. At the standard metabolic temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C], the time since birth at first brood is 365 days [tR = 365 days], although as noted, actual breeding is frequently deferred. This combination of a small clutch size of two eggs [N_R_i = clutch size of two eggs] and a high annual frequency of 2.8 clutches per year [F_R_i = 2.8 clutches per year] results in a modest but sustained reproductive output across a long adult lifespan. The strategy appears well-suited to the stable, food-limited environment of the montane forest, where adults can reliably produce a few high-quality offspring each year rather than gambling on a single large brood. The Puaiohi's persistence in the face of habitat fragmentation and introduced predators is a testament to this resilient life-history framework.
